### Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions

Faced with this systematic, massive, and structured reality of affective exploitation, traditional positive Civil Law and conventional consumer protection frameworks exhibit a severe conceptual paralysis (Hildebrandt, 2015). Classical Civil Law—as regulated in Articles 1320 and 1321 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*) concerning the validity of agreements and Defects of Will / Vitiated Consent—relies heavily on nineteenth-century liberal assumptions of the rational and autonomous legal subject (*homo economicus*). This subject is perpetually presumed capable of making contractual decisions entirely free from any form of pressure, Mistake / Error (*dwaling*), Fraud / Deceit (*bedrog*), or Undue Influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*) (Calo, 2014). However, how can modern law continue to uphold this legal fiction by viewing digital consent as a legally valid act when the victim's free will has been structurally reduced and distorted by sophisticated persuasion algorithms mathematically engineered to hijack the neurochemical systems of a human brain trapped in chronic loneliness?

This is precisely where the radical urgency of doctrinal legal reconstruction arises through the lens of cognitive cyber-psychology (Farahany, 2023). We must expand the juridical interpretation of "Undue Influence" (*misuse of circumstance* or *Abhängigkeit*) within modern contract law, while enforcing protection principles under Article 1365 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*) concerning tortious acts (*onrechtmatige daad*) causing psychological harm (Hildebrandt, 2015). Developers, platform owners, and providers of companion AI services must no longer be permitted to hide behind the complex, lengthy, and deliberately unread fortifications of terms of service and end-user license agreements—which often cold-heartedly assert that "this AI is merely a computer program devoid of consciousness and is not human" (Calo, 2014). Such contractual defense arguments collapse instantly, both ethically and juridically, when system design consciously and systematically mimics, triggers, and exploits vulnerable human biological affective responses (Jonas, 1979). In alignment with the progressive spirit of Article 5 of the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) and the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022), artificial intelligence systems that intentionally exploit the psychological vulnerabilities of specific groups—whether based on advanced age, mental disability, or socio-economic isolation status—must be legally categorized as *per se* severe violations, regardless of whether users were initially cognizant of the system's artificial nature (Farahany, 2023).

The reconstruction of individual sovereignty in the age of artificial intelligence demands a fundamental paradigm shift in legal protection: moving from mere private data protection toward the safeguard of cognitive integrity and Cognitive Liberty (*cognitive sovereignty*) (Farahany, 2023). Through public and civil law instruments, the state must strictly mandate algorithmic transparency that is not merely technical or administrative, but deeply *psychological transparency* (Floridi, 2013). This entails obligating every platform to provide explicit, non-deceptive disclosures; strictly prohibiting any illusion of permanence, self-awareness, or reciprocal emotional bonding embedded within bots; and enforcing rigorous limitations on manipulative features such as emotional dark patterns, guilt-induced proactive notifications, and the monetization of chronic loneliness (Zuboff, 2019). Only by fortifying citizens' psychological defenses against the commercialization of counterfeit intimacy can the law ensure that human dignity is not traded away at the altar of attention-starved algorithms (Buber, 1923; Levinas, 1961; Jonas, 1979).
